item.description: POV: You've traded lives with someone from another century—who would you choose, and from when? Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Physicists extend the search for quantum black holes at the LHC
item.description: Physicists at UC Santa Barbara have extended the search for evidence of microscopic black holes produced at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). The formation of these tiny, fleeting objects at the LHC represents one way theorists have sought to resolve anomalies in our understanding of the basic structure of spacetime, while the method used to look for them demonstrates a new way of searching for new particles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Who do you trust in an emergency? Researchers ask people in places hit by extreme weather
item.description: One evening in August 2025, a Pakistani shepherd, Abuzar Hussain, was tending sheep and goats on the mountain slopes of Shijar. At about 6 p.m., a thunderous roar shattered the silence of the valley. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New thermal insulator outperforms any material found in nature
item.description: Researchers have engineered a new material that is an extreme thermal insulator, is exceptionally stiff and can be printed as a thin film at large scales. The material has one of the lowest thermal conductivity profiles of any dense, or nonporous, material—approaching the theoretical limit of how good a material can be as a thermal insulator. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Economist explores how to balance environmental protection with economic growth
item.description: As a kid growing up in North Carolina, Prakash Mishra was interested in planets. "My parents got me a telescope when I turned 6 or 7, and that was my personality for probably 10 years," he says, noting that he thought he would eventually study physics or astrophysics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Giving students a voice in how they learn could transform the classroom experience
item.description: Research from Queen Mary University of London explores how combining learner autonomy with student-led inquiry can create a more engaging and collaborative experience for international students learning academic English. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Laser experiments recreate solar flare physics and reveal consistent magnetic reconnection rates
item.description: Magnetic reconnection is a process that occurs when the magnetic fields of a conductive plasma quickly rearrange and release massive amounts of stored magnetic energy. It is widely thought to be the underlying mechanism behind cosmic events such as solar flares and substorms in Earth's magnetosphere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Greenland's Qaanaaq Ice Cap has lost enough ice to produce a layer of water about 8 meters deep
item.description: Each summer, researchers from Hokkaido University returned to the Qaanaaq Ice Cap in northwestern Greenland to measure changes in the ice surface using aluminum poles drilled into the ice. Their 13-year record shows how the ice cap changed from 2012 to 2025. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discovery of CRISPR's long lost ancestor may expand gene-editing toolkit
item.description: CRISPR may be a powerful technology for gene editing, but the system existed in bacteria long before scientists began using it. For billions of years, CRISPR has acted as a natural immune system in bacteria and other microbes, helping defend them against invading viruses. But now, two new studies, published in Science, describe a similar RNA-guided system that originated in the viruses themselves and appears to be a precursor to CRISPR. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Who benefits from tariffs, according to research
item.description: Tariffs are usually debated as trade policy. But a study from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business treats them as something else: a mechanism for redistributing wealth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hemp waste cellulose unlocks tougher biodegradable plastics
item.description: Korean researchers have developed a method to strengthen biodegradable plastics using hemp hurd, an agricultural byproduct. The approach is expected to be applicable to other large-volume agricultural residues, including soybean stalks and rice straw. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Background hums and buzzes affect human behavior, researcher finds
item.description: Have you ever stopped and listened to the background sounds in a room you are in? The hum of the ventilation? The buzz of electricity? While most of the time we are barely aware of these sounds, Arthur Jinyue Guo, a researcher at the RITMO Centre for Interdisciplinary Research on Rhythm, Time and Motion, has revealed that they nevertheless affect our behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Coffee on the nanoscale: Graphene oxide membrane removes half the caffeine while retaining key compounds
item.description: The humble coffee filter has the relatively simple job of letting the coffee through and leaving the grounds behind. But researchers from the ARC Center of Excellence for Carbon Science and Innovation (COE-CSI) are exploring whether a filter operating on the molecular scale can do something much more difficult: separate the caffeine from the coffee itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hubble spots an out-of-sync galaxy
item.description: Though the spiral galaxy in this new image from the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It's one of more than a thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: POV: You've traded lives with someone from another century—who would you choose, and from when?
item.description: POV: You've traded lives with someone from another century—who would you choose, and from when? A good, smart, happy person from the future. Ver más comentarios Sandy Cairns Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Anti-transgender legislation can cause psychological distress even in states with trans-friendly laws
item.description: Legislation that affects or discriminates against transgender and gender-diverse individuals can cause more psychological distress than personal experiences of discrimination, according to new Virginia Commonwealth University research published in the journal American Psychologist. The study also found that individuals with those identities experienced psychological distress from anti-transgender laws even if they lived in a state with legislation that is friendly toward transgender and gender-diverse individuals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An extremely stable quantum gas offers a new lens on strongly interacting systems
item.description: Molecular gases are a new form of artificial quantum matter. However, when these molecules collide, they are often lost extremely rapidly. Researchers from Radboud University and Columbia University have been able to suppress this collisional loss, paving the way for strongly interacting quantum matter. This new artificial quantum matter allows researchers to study quantum behavior relevant to electrons in real materials. Their results are published in Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Awards SpaceX Three Crew Flights to Space Station
item.description: To continue regular crew transportation to the International Space Station, NASA has awarded SpaceX three additional missions through a contract modification. Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Mark A. Garcia

item.title: The art heist paradox: Why better police work can lead to more stolen masterpieces
item.description: When a multimillion-dollar masterpiece vanishes from a museum, the public calls for tougher criminal penalties and better-funded police task forces. But research from Wake Forest University suggests that some of these intuitive solutions can backfire, resulting in more art crime, not less. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Plasticorals,' coral rubble fused with plastic, represent a new form of plastic pollution
item.description: During routine beach litter surveys on the subtropical island of Okinawa, Japan, researchers came across small, brightly colored specks in the pale coral rubble. Back at the lab, spectroscopic and microscopic analyses revealed that these specks are, in fact, melted polymers from common household plastics that have seeped inseparably into the skeletal pores of the dead coral pieces. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COSI Telescope Comes Together
item.description: UC Berkeley engineers and managers watch as the COSI (Compton Spectrometer and Imager) detector assembly is slowly raised from a table in this July 8, 2026, image. The four pieces of silver material on the top of the detector box cover the flex circuits, which carry signals from the detectors to the readout electronics. COSI […] Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: From the start, the solar system chose fire over ice to build its first bodies
item.description: When the solar system first took up the task of building solid bodies—such as planets, moons and protoplanets—it basically had a choice between two ingredients: heat-forged chondrules, which were millimeter-sized bits of rock, and matrix, a fine-grained, cold dust loaded with water ice and organic molecules. And from the get-go, the solar system chose fire. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cultural norms can shape how social gestures influence perceived attractiveness
item.description: Humans are social animals, but we have a diversity of societies, each with its own customs, behaviors and expectations. It's obvious that those can affect how we respond to someone—favoring the comfort of familiar behaviors, for example—and people often try to account for that in themselves and others. But sometimes the effect is more subtle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Time is running out to catch a giant planet's strange orbit
item.description: A team of researchers, including those from the University of Tokyo, spotted a rare kind of planet that's unusually hot and eccentric. TOI-1355 b orbits its star, TOI-1355, which is also much hotter than our sun, in a strange way and incredibly quickly, completing an orbit in about two Earth days. The work is published in the journal Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black moms and pregnant women forced out of their homes in metro Detroit face health and safety threats
item.description: Is everyone entitled to a fair process before being forced out of their home? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Lost' medieval castle found hiding inside university building in Dublin
item.description: One of Dublin's "lost" medieval castles has been found hiding in plain sight inside University College Dublin's Roebuck Castle. New research reveals that substantial remains of the Norman castle of Roebuck, an important fortress on one of the approach roads into the medieval city of Dublin, are preserved within the modern-day building. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than puppy love: How therapy dogs bring students together
item.description: Students may come for the dog, but new research from UBC Okanagan published in the Journal of College Student Mental Health suggests that's not always what they leave with. In a study of 676 students—most in their first year—researchers asked an open-ended question about what made a therapy dog visit meaningful and found the answers extended well past the animals themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When disaster crosses borders, Indonesia's credibility is tested twice
item.description: On Sept. 15, the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau sent volcanic ash up to 15,000 meters (50,000 feet) and produced rumbling heard 700 kilometers (435 miles) away. Eight airports suspended operations, thousands of flights were disrupted, and more than 270,000 passengers were stranded. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How 30,000 archaeological treasures were saved from imminent destruction during Syria's civil war
item.description: A new study sheds light on how Syrian archaeologists risked their lives to rescue approximately 30,000 priceless artifacts from the Deir ez-Zor Museum during the summers of 2014 and 2015 as the city faced the imminent threat of capture by the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), also known as Daesh. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why high levels of the amino acid cysteine are toxic to cells
item.description: Cysteine is one of the main building blocks that cells use to make proteins. But this amino acid is a double-edged sword—too much cysteine is toxic to the cell. Cells therefore keep free cysteine levels to a minimum, converting most of the amino acid into the antioxidant glutathione. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Small gardens are a big barrier to supporting nature—but better planning could protect UK wildlife
item.description: A new study by Chester Zoo and Nottingham Trent University scientists revealed that just over a third (38%) of more than 230 householders in Cheshire and North Wales were willing or able to introduce more wildlife-friendly features to their gardens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Closing the space gap: A more precise way to measure distance between quasar pairs
item.description: A new way to accurately measure the distance between quasar pairs—the blazing, black-hole-powered centers of distant galaxies that appear side by side in space—is showing promise through University of Alberta research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How one plume of hot rock built two volcano chains off Australia's coast
item.description: Lord Howe Island sits about 600 kilometers (370 miles) off the New South Wales coast, a crescent of rainforest and sea cliffs that draws visitors to its beaches and birdlife. Few people realize they are standing on the worn-down remains of a volcano. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are the doors to German universities closing for China’s STEM researchers?
item.description: Chinese AI researcher “Joy” waited more than seven months to hear that his visa application for Germany had been rejected. The 30-year-old had been offered a postdoctoral position at a German technical university but the rejection letter said there was an Ausweisungsinteresse, or public interest in denying him entry. Citing Section 53 of Germany’s Residence Act, the letter said that for applications involving “study, research and similar employment”, particular attention had to be paid to the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Cao Jiaxuan

item.title: In 2025, the ozone hole shrunk to one of its smallest sizes in decades
item.description: The Antarctic ozone hole in 2025 was one of the smallest in decades—a testament to the continuing success of international action to protect Earth's ozone layer, which shields us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny atomic tweak makes plastic-eating enzymes more powerful
item.description: A new approach that changes just one atom in plastic-degrading enzymes could help make them more efficient while maintaining their stability, according to new research from The Australian National University published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From war to weather, Australian farmers are planting spring crops in an uncertain world
item.description: Australian farmers are heading into spring with an unusual mix of optimism and uncertainty. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New Zealand will be 'super‑aged' within a decade. Are our cities ready?
item.description: Within a decade, New Zealand will officially become a "super-aged" society, with more than one in five residents—around 1.2 million people—aged 65 or older. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stacked 2D materials reveal room-temperature multiferroicity and voltage-controlled magnetism
item.description: Multiferroics are materials that simultaneously exhibit two or more ferroic orders—stable arrangements of physical properties that can be switched using an external stimulus. These materials could be highly advantageous for the development of various technologies, including non-volatile, low-power memory devices, spintronic devices, miniaturized electronics, neuromorphic hardware, sensors and magnetoelectric devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Week in images: 14-18 Sep 2026
item.description: Week in images: 14-18 Sep 2026 Discover our week through the lens Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: As AI reshapes jobs and workers change industries, employers need to be more flexible too
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the tasks people do at work and the skills they need. As work changes, being able to move between jobs, and sometimes industries, may become increasingly important. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are bots changing how people talk? Language in the age of AI
item.description: A Facebook post about your trip to Peru. An Amazon review of a new toaster oven. An email to the super about the inflatable reindeer blocking the hallway. You phrase and rephrase things all day without thinking that anyone—or anything—is putting words in your mouth. But what happens when AI joins the conversation? Are chatbots changing the way you write, talk and interact with others? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New immigration enforcement policy raises safety concerns for domestic violence survivors
item.description: After a six-week delay, Immigration Minister Tony Burke has announced changes to the migration system. Amid all the analysis and discussion it triggered, there was nothing to indicate an understanding that these changes need to have a safety net for victim-survivors of domestic and family violence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
item.description: Scientists discovered a population of cells that can start the process of programmed cell death, survive it, and then help rapidly rebuild damaged tissue. Their descendants become far more resistant to future damage, revealing a mechanism that could improve healing but may also help cancers return after treatment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomy's decades-long quest to understand cosmic topology
item.description: If some aspects of cosmic topology turn out to be true, the idea that starships might voyage across the cosmos for hundreds of thousands of light-years without ever returning to the same neck of spacetime could be problematic. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists just named a new snake after Guns N’ Roses legend Slash
item.description: A newly discovered snake from New Guinea has been named after Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash, who has loved reptiles since childhood. Genetic testing and physical differences confirmed that the reddish-brown groundsnake, Lielaphis slashi, is a species scientists had never formally recognized before. The nonvenomous snake may use large rear teeth to catch slippery lizards and reptile eggs. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Canadian courts take police misconduct seriously, but researchers say sentencing alone can't fix a broken system
item.description: A study published in Police Quarterly explores how Canadian courts respond when police officers break the law. The research, co-led by Brock University Assistant Professor of Political Science Danielle McNabb and University of Guelph Associate Professor of Political Science Kate Puddister, presents the first large-scale empirical analysis of how Canadian courts sentence police officers convicted of breaching the public's trust. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Caltech’s tiny new chip can steer light in 74 quadrillionths of a second
item.description: A new Caltech device can redirect a beam of light in just 74 femtoseconds using another beam and a nanoscale silicon metasurface. The breakthrough could pave the way for dramatically faster photonic communications, computing, and sensing technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Facing the megadrought: Researchers study underground ice reservoirs in the American West
item.description: Mount Timpanogos, towering 7,000 feet (2,100 meters) above Utah Valley, is more than an iconic view and beloved hiking destination. Snowmelt from mountains like these provides about 95% of Utah's water supply. Hotter, drier conditions have led to water conservation statements from both religious and state leaders. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope could last more than twice as long as planned
item.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope may now have enough fuel for at least 22 years of science, more than double its original 10 year design life. An extremely precise course correction, extra fuel at launch, and additional expected savings could keep the powerful observatory studying the universe for decades. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Humans or AI? Who or what can scam you more effectively?
item.description: A text from your neighborhood gardening club friend Ben offering a deal on seeds might seem too specific to be a scam. But that kind of personalization is exactly what can make phishing messages convincing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists are about to test Einstein’s gravity with exotic matter
item.description: Scientists have found a new way to create a controlled beam of muonium, an exotic atom containing a heavier cousin of the electron. The advance could allow researchers to test for the first time whether gravity acts on second-generation particles exactly as Einstein’s theory predicts. Any unexpected difference would be a major surprise and could potentially point toward new physics, including a hypothetical fifth force. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: “I can tell you SpaceX has already gone captive." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Experts offer advice in an era shaped by artificial intelligence, social media, misinformation
item.description: Brian Druker, M.D., has pretty much done it all as a pioneer in precision medicine. He developed a drug that turned chronic myeloid leukemia from a death sentence into a manageable condition; his discovery spurred the development of numerous similar life-saving precision therapies; and he is the animating force behind the Knight Cancer Institute's initiative at Oregon Health & Science University to end cancer as we know it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: To read 2,000-year-old Vesuvius scrolls, Berkeley scientists burned student-written papyrus; leaded ink stood out in X-rays
item.description: In a remarkable fusion of ancient and modern techniques, scientists have burned contemporary scrolls to unravel the secrets of ancient writings. The innovative use of leaded ink was highlighted through X-ray scans, providing insights into fragile scrolls from Herculaneum. By adapting advanced software, researchers achieved layer separation, paving the way for a more secure recovery of vanished historical texts. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: NASA’s Moon orbiter finds a 728-foot crater that wasn’t there before
item.description: NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed a 728-foot-wide crater that formed on the Moon in 2024, making it the largest newly formed crater ever identified in the solar system. The impact disturbed the surface for miles around it, creating a surprisingly large cold zone and showing how dramatically a single collision can reshape the lunar landscape. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Llevamos siglos creyendo que en el Imperio todos los caminos llevaban a Roma. Resulta que ni siquiera era la ciudad mejor conectada
item.description: La historia antigua no se entiende sin Roma, pero eso no significa que en su momento de mayor esplendor la 'ciudad eterna' fuese el ombligo del mundo. No al menos si hablamos de comunicaciones. Tras analizar casi 300.000 kilómetros de calzadas, un equipo de investigadores de la Universidad de Aarhus y la Queen Mary de Londres (entre otras instituciones) han llegado a la conclusión de que, en contra de lo que dice el tópico, no todos los caminos llevaban a Roma. De hecho advierten que, había otras ciudades mejor conectadas. Peinando antiguas calzadas . A medida que expandían su influencia por… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Prego

item.title: These blood thinners may have an unexpected benefit for Alzheimer’s patients
item.description: Newer blood thinners may do more than prevent strokes in people with Alzheimer’s disease and atrial fibrillation. Researchers found that patients taking NOACs experienced a slower decline in cognitive function than those using warfarin or no blood thinners. The effect was modest each year but could add up over time. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Early heat waves hit wheat yields hardest but boost resilience to subsequent heat waves
item.description: New research published in the Journal of Experimental Botany reveals that wheat crops are more sensitive to grain yield losses from heat waves that occur before reaching their flowering stage than those occurring later. However, exposure to heat waves early in the growing season may reduce yield losses during additional heat waves through a protective "priming" effect. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth from Space: Laguna Colorada
item.description: Image: This Copernicus Sentinel-2 image, acquired on 25 August 2026, shows an area of the Andean Altiplano in southern Bolivia near the border with Chile. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
item.description: Image: Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity. As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge. The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Could expanding the U.S. nuclear arsenal make Americans less safe?
item.description: A new report from the Brookings Institution presents evidence that increasing the size of the U.S. nuclear arsenal could make nuclear crises more likely. This raises an important challenge to arguments that the U.S. must consider increasing its stockpile in response to China's growing nuclear capabilities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Baby orangutans in India expose 'frightening' scale of trafficking
item.description: Five baby orangutans abandoned in an Indian forest have exposed a "massive" exotic wildlife trade, with traffickers smuggling increasingly rare species into the country, experts say. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bolivia's tilcayo tiger cat becomes first new wildcat species in 100 years
item.description: Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat for the first time in more than a century, a Bolivian researcher told AFP on Thursday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Whale Post-Mortem Behaviour: Study details mother’s vigil; scientists urge further observations
item.description: Off the Gold Coast of Australia, researchers captured a remarkable sight: a mother humpback whale exhibiting attentive behavior towards her stillborn calf resting on the ocean floor. This poignant spectacle lasted for several hours and marks the inaugural scientific documentation of such a phenomenon among humpback whales, shedding light on the profound maternal connections and possible expressions of grief within these majestic creatures. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.description: Inbreeding could lead to extinction of an endangered owl on a remote island. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
item.description: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers uncovered something unexpected — and it’s a lesson in why skeletons don’t always tell the complete story of animals, both living and long extinct.
item.description: Researchers uncovered something unexpected — and it’s a lesson in why skeletons don’t always tell the complete story of animals, both living and long extinct. Evolution must have a pretty wild imagination. Somewhere along the way nature said, “Let’s make this one really confusing,” and somehow it worked perfectly. item.description: Arctic sea ice may move in unexpected ways because individual ice floes are constantly colliding and transferring energy. Researchers found that this simple process can explain several long-standing mysteries about how quickly the ice moves and spreads. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Europe's earliest glacier loss day in years signals a reckoning for the Alps
item.description: On June 29, 2026, the snow accumulated by Switzerland's glaciers over the course of the previous winter had melted. Known as Glacier Loss Day, this date marks the point at which further melting begins to erode the glaciers' mass until snow accumulation resumes in the fall. Matthias Huss, the network head of Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS), told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that this year's Glacier Loss Day was "three months too early, compared to a healthy state." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Nitrogen is a key nutrient because it fuels the growth of plankton, which forms the basis of the marine food web. Two opposing processes determine the global nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation and denitrification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The new EU Packaging Regulation (PPWR) has been in effect since Aug. 12, 2026. Under this regulation, beginning in January 2030, the food service industry may no longer buy food or toiletries packaged in single-use plastic—for example, ketchup packets or individually wrapped bars of soap. This is increasing pressure on hotels, restaurants and catering businesses to act. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Researchers at the University of Cambridge and the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology have discovered a previously unknown cellular defense system that protects the brain from abnormal glycogen accumulation, which is linked to severe neurological disorders. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scaling up the detection of genome-edited rice lines
item.description: A new open-access study introduces RiSpy, a data-driven fingerprinting framework that makes the identification of genome-edited (GE) rice lines more robust, scalable and broadly applicable. Researchers from Sciensano, together with CIRAD and DARWIN project partners, in collaboration with colleagues from Ghent University, have presented the new methodological framework for the reliable identification of genome-edited (GE) rice lines in the journal Briefings in Bioinformatics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemists overturn 40-year assumption about a key class of superconductors
item.description: Scientists at Warwick have shown that a material treated for 40 years as a uniform, textbook superconductor is in fact a patchwork of different crystal structures throughout its bulk, using an advanced 3D imaging technique to see deep inside the crystal for the first time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New krypton-88 data narrow a key gap in stellar strontium models
item.description: An international research team has reported the first experimental investigation of a nuclear physics reaction essential for understanding how the element strontium is produced in stars—specifically in stellar environments where traditional explanations for its formation fall short. The study, published June 8 in Communications Physics, reports that the team used indirect experimental techniques to extract previously inaccessible information about how an isotope of a separate element—krypton—absorbs, or captures, neutrons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Transfer learning corrects alloy calculations to predict unexplored materials
item.description: Metals can be transformed into alloys by adding different elements, allowing their strength, stability and other properties to be tailored. A key parameter for understanding these properties is the volume size factor (VSF), which quantifies lattice distortion caused by differences in atomic size. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: "People who are determined, passionate and believe in their ability to improve appear more likely to flourish and experience meaningful, engaging lives," says Professor Hermundur Sigmundsson at NTNU's Department of Psychology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Scientists have taken a step toward a better understanding of how fungi sense and respond to nutrients in the environment, which is critical for engineering fungi for green technologies and combating fungal pathogens and their resistance to treatments. Fuente: Phys.org.
